title: Translating Flow to Policy via Hindsight Online Imitation
one_liner: When a robot tries an action and moves some points on a video, relabel that movement as the goal and train the low-level policy to imitate it — turning any outcome into a lesson.
lead: Most robot learning relies on having many expert-labeled demonstrations (examples of what actions to take). This paper proposes a different path: the robot tries actions online, and for every outcome that actually happened, the method retroactively decides what those point movements (called flows) were the goal, then trains the policy to reproduce them next time. This turns every failed or partial attempt into a lesson without needing a human to label it.

problem.h2: The grounding problem: plans are not actions
paras: Today's robot systems work in two layers: a high-level planner (trained on videos, which show movement but not how the robot's joints move) proposes where things should go, and a low-level policy (trained on robot data, which is scarce and expensive) figures out what joint commands achieve that. The bottleneck is the low-level policy — it needs hundreds of labeled examples showing which actions lead to which outcomes.

A beginner might try: collect 100 robot attempts, ask a human to label each action, and train directly. This works, but humans are slow, expensive, and inconsistent. When you have only 2 or 5 labeled examples, the policy overfits and fails on new tasks. The unspoken trap: the planner sees task-relevant motion in videos (e.g., a hand sliding toward a cube), but the policy never learns to produce that exact motion unless someone manually annotates it.

callout.html: After the robot takes an action and something moves, treat the movement it actually achieved as the intended goal, and train the policy to copy it next time.

panels.title: 1. Robot acts blind
panels.caption: Low-level policy has no goal. It guesses an action blindly.

panels.title: 2. Something moves
panels.caption: Action is taken, points on the video shift. What happened is now visible.

panels.title: 3. Hindsight asks: What was the goal?
panels.caption: Instead of asking humans, the method asks: those points that moved — call that the goal.

panels.title: 4. Pair action with goal
panels.caption: Now we have action plus goal. Train the policy to match action to that flow.

panels.title: 5. Policy learns from its own attempts
panels.caption: The policy no longer needs human labels. It learns from every attempt it makes.

steps.text: Train a flow predictor (a model that learns which points move how far) using 100 action-free videos and no robot data at all.
Get a weak low-level policy by training on only 2 labeled robot demonstrations of the task.
Let the policy interact with the real robot for 80,000 steps, trying actions and observing what happens.
For each rollout, extract the actual point movements (flows) from the video, and call those the goal the policy was trying to achieve.
Train the policy to take the observed image plus that hindsight goal and predict the action that was actually taken. Repeat online.

paras: The paper changes how the low-level policy learns: instead of waiting for a human to label the goal after an action, the method uses the movement that actually occurred as the retroactive goal. This turns the policy into a goal-conditioned imitator that learns from its own outcomes.

hidden.name: Point flow (how far task-relevant points move)
paras: The paper measures a specific hidden quantity that a beginner would overlook: the flow is the distance and direction that certain pixels on the video shift between one frame and the next. For example, if a hand is sliding a cube, the hand's position in the image moves from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) — that is the flow. It is not the robot's joint angles (which differ between embodiments), and it is not a language label like 'push' (which is ambiguous). It is the concrete, observable motion in 2D pixel space.

The paper estimates flow by running a flow-prediction model (pretrained on videos) on the actual video frames after each robot action, then finding which points moved the most. The hindsight insight: instead of asking 'what was the intended goal?', the method treats the measured flow as ground truth — the goal the policy should have been trying to hit all along.

heat.caption: Darker cells are task-relevant points that moved most; these define the achieved goal.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the flow: which video pixels shifted, and by how much. It is what the high-level planner predicts, and it is what the low-level policy learns to produce.

The method extracts point flow from the video dataset by applying a task-centric point sampler to select query points and then tracking their future trajectories. The flow prediction loss ensures the high-level planner accurately predicts future trajectories of task-relevant points.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: hindsight closes the annotation gap
paras: The core mechanism is deceptively simple: every action the robot takes produces an outcome. That outcome is visible — the camera shows exactly which points moved. Normally, that outcome is discarded if it was not what a human expected. But the paper notices: even if the outcome was a mistake, it is still ground truth. The policy can learn from it by asking 'if I take this action and see this image, which flow will I produce?' — and the answer is: the flow I actually produced.

Why this breaks the sample-efficiency problem: with only 2 labeled examples, the policy is weak and will make mistakes. Those mistakes give bad outcomes — but bad outcomes are still data. Each mistake, when relabeled retroactively as a goal and paired with the action that caused it, becomes a valid training example. The policy learns not just from expert demos but from its own failures, because failures reveal real cause-and-effect. In 80,000 online steps, the policy collects thousands of self-generated goal labels, requiring zero additional human work.

stages.s: Next frame observed; flow extracted from video
Retroactively treat flow as the goal the policy was targeting
Retraining: learn to predict this action given image and this flow

math.h2: The math: supervised learning with hindsight goals
math.words: Loss = sum over all online steps of (predicted_action - actual_action) squared, where the policy gets to see both the current image and the achieved flow as extra input to guide its prediction.
symbols: the policy function: predicts what action to take given observation o_t and hindsight goal g_t
the current robot observation (camera image and joint positions at timestep t)
the hindsight goal: the flow that was actually achieved (pixel movement from the video)
the action the robot actually took at timestep t
squared error: how far off the prediction was

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Timestep 1: Policy sees image, gets flow goal showing hand moved 20 pixels right and 15 down. Policy predicts action (0.8, 0.6). Robot actually took action (0.9, 0.7). Error = (0.8-0.9)^2 + (0.6-0.7)^2 = 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02.
Timestep 3: Policy predicts (0.85, 0.65). Robot took (0.85, 0.65). Error = 0.
As the policy trains, it learns to predict the action more accurately by using the flow as a guide — the policy realizes which actions produce which flows.

math.note: The hindsight goal acts as a supervision signal: the policy learns to match the action to the flow that was observed, without waiting for a human to label that flow.

charts.title: Naive approach (human labeling)
charts.note: Performance drops steeply when human labels run out.

charts.title: HinFlow (hindsight relabeling)
charts.note: Online relabeling provides thousands of goals; performance stays high even with minimal human data.

items.b: Compounding errors if the flow predictor is weak.
items.html: If the high-level planner (flow predictor) was trained on bad video data or makes wild guesses about which points matter, the hindsight goals it assigns will mislead the policy. The policy will learn correlations that do not match the task.

items.b: Catastrophic forgetting when online steps start producing very different flows.
items.html: If the policy learns a different strategy than the pretraining videos showed, the flow patterns may shift so far that the flow predictor's guesses become unreliable. The hindsight labels degrade, and learning stalls.

items.b: Noise in early online steps can pollute the training signal.
items.html: In the first few rollouts, the weak policy may take random actions and produce random flows. If the method labels these as legitimate goals without filtering, it creates contradictory training data — 'this image should produce both very different actions depending on noise.'
Start with a plausible pretrained policy and plausible video data. Use exploration noise strategically (not too much, not too little). Aggregate over many online steps so random noise averages out.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show that starting with only 2 labeled robot examples, 80,000 online rollouts, and a flow predictor trained on action-free videos, the policy learns to solve a manipulation task (e.g., pushing a cube to a target location or picking up an object). It should directly compare: without hindsight relabeling (i.e., trying to train without the retroactive goal labels), the same 2 examples and the same 80,000 steps lead to much worse performance, proving that hindsight is what enabled learning.
demo.metric_eq: Task success rate = (number of rollouts that reached the goal) / (total number of final 10 rollouts)
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that the policy never saw a human telling it 'this flow is correct' after the first 2 examples — it learned by relabeling its own outcomes. That is the core contribution.
